name: Morpheus8 (RF microneedling)

card.summary: InMode fractional radiofrequency microneedling device marketed for skin tightening and subdermal fat remodeling along the jawline and neck; evidence is mainly case series and reviews.
card.note: Grokipedia reports the FDA has noted risks such as burns, scarring and unintended fat loss with RF microneedling; a 2026 paper describes fibrosis and surgical complexity after nonsurgical treatments.

quick.overview:
Morpheus8 is a handheld device from InMode that combines microneedling with bipolar radiofrequency (RF) energy. Needles penetrate the skin to set depths and deliver heat to the dermis and subdermal layers, with the stated aims of stimulating collagen, tightening skin and remodeling a small amount of fat.
It is used on the face and neck, including the jawline and jowls, as a lower-downtime option for mild to moderate laxity. Reviews and retrospective series report improvements, but no randomized comparison against surgery exists.
quick.mechanism: Insulated microneedles create channels in the skin while RF energy heats tissue at depths that Grokipedia says reach up to 8 mm. The resulting controlled injury is described as triggering a healing response with new collagen, and deeper settings are said to coagulate subdermal fat. It is often combined with FaceTite or liposuction.
quick.risks: Described risks include burns, scarring, pigmentation changes and unintended fat loss. A 2026 surgical paper reports that fibrosis and fat loss after nonsurgical treatments can complicate later neck lift surgery.

lead: Morpheus8 is a fractional radiofrequency microneedling device made by InMode that combines microneedles with bipolar RF energy to heat the dermis and subdermal tissue. Manufacturers and practitioners describe it as promoting collagen production, tightening skin and remodeling adipose tissue on the face, neck and body.[1][2]

It grew out of InMode's Fractora fractional RF platform; a 2020 study describes a combination of FaceTite bipolar RF and a fractional bipolar RF device (Fractora modified to Morpheus8) for lower face and neck laxity.[3] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports commercial introduction around 2018, US FDA clearance in 2020 for electrocoagulation and hemostasis, and a further clearance in 2024 for soft tissue contraction.[1]

Reviews in dermatology and facial plastic surgery present RF microneedling as a minimally invasive option for skin laxity, acne scarring and rejuvenation,[2][4] while the published evidence on jawline and fat remodeling consists largely of retrospective series and combination reports.[3][5][6]

For people interested in a sharper jawline and firmer neck, the appeal of RF microneedling is that it targets laxity without an incision: it is done in an office, usually with topical numbing, and is promoted as having less downtime than a facelift or neck lift.[2][4] Practitioners often position it for people in a treatment gap between those who need only skin care and those who need an excisional procedure, a group described in a 2019 case series of combined RF treatments.[7]

paras: A 2022 review in Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology describes Morpheus8 as fractional RF microneedling that treats concerns from skin laxity to acne and scarring with reduced downtime compared with historically more invasive approaches.[2] A second 2022 review, in facial plastic surgery, states that RF microneedling is considered a safe and effective treatment for various aesthetic and dermatologic conditions in all skin types and highlights what differentiates Morpheus8 from other devices.[4]

Grokipedia reports several tip configurations, including resurfacing, intermediate and deep subdermal tips and a body tip, and says treatment depth is adjustable.[1] Because this source is AI-generated, device specifications should be checked against the manufacturer.

A 2020 retrospective review evaluated FaceTite bipolar RF combined with a fractional bipolar RF device modified to Morpheus8 for laxity of the lower face and neck.[3] A 2019 paper on adjustable-depth fractional RF with bipolar RF describes the combination as a treatment for patients between younger patients wanting tightening without surgery and those with laxity not severe enough for an excisional procedure.[7] A 2021 paper reported using RF-assisted lipolysis with RF microneedling for premature jowl and neck laxity after face-lift surgery.[5]
A 2025 paper describes combining low-energy Morpheus8 with nanofat grafting for compartment-specific facial rejuvenation, reporting selective fat remodeling and skin quality enhancement.[8]

Fractional RF has also been studied in acne and scarring and in hidradenitis suppurativa. A 2025 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal examined fractional RF for long-term acne remission and reduction of acne scar load,[9] and a 2026 retrospective study in Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology reported on fractional microneedling RF in hidradenitis suppurativa across anatomical sites.[10]

Grokipedia reports that the FDA has noted risks of RF microneedling devices including burns, scarring and unintended fat loss.[1] A 2026 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal describes fibrosis, fat loss and increased surgical complexity in patients who undergo neck lift after nonsurgical treatments.[11] A 2024 review discusses the role of noninvasive and minimally invasive techniques alongside open surgical procedures for body contouring.[12]

Common short-term effects described in reviews include redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and tenderness; less common events include burns, scarring and pigment change, which is why settings and technique matter.[2][14] A 2026 Aesthetic Surgery Journal study of patients undergoing secondary neck lift reported fibrosis, tissue destruction and anatomical change after prior noninvasive neck treatments, including energy-based devices, that increased surgical complexity.[11]

Standard microneedling uses fine needles to create small mechanical injuries that prompt the skin to repair itself; Wikipedia notes that this collagen induction approach has been used for scarring, acne and, in some studies, hair loss.[13] RF microneedling adds electrical energy delivered through the needles. A 2019 overview in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics of North America says RF microneedling devices allow more aggressive treatments with minimal downtime compared with earlier RF devices, and that optimizing treatment parameters is essential to safety and efficacy.[14]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes insulated needles that deliver bipolar RF energy at adjustable depths of up to 8 mm, producing small heat zones separated by untreated skin so the surface heals quickly. It attributes tightening to fibroblast activation and new collagen and elastin, and says deeper settings coagulate small amounts of subdermal fat, a feature the manufacturer markets as subdermal adipose remodeling.[1] Tip configurations vary by area, from shallow tips for surface texture to deeper tips for the lower face and neck.[1]

Reviews describe a series of sessions rather than a single treatment, usually with topical anesthesia, followed by temporary redness, swelling and pinpoint marks that settle over days.[2][4] Results are described as developing gradually over weeks to months as collagen remodeling proceeds.[1][2] Clinics frequently pair the device with other treatments: subdermal RF devices such as FaceTite or AccuTite for fat and laxity, platelet-rich plasma or growth-factor products applied after needling, or fat grafting.[3][8][15][16]

Surgeons who use RF devices in body contouring describe them as complements to surgery as well as alternatives. A 2024 Clinics in Plastic Surgery article by a practising surgeon lists Morpheus8 among RF procedures used for skin tightening, alongside FaceTite, BodyTite and AccuTite.[12] A 2020 review on noninvasive abdominoplasty notes that high equipment costs, conflicting anecdotal reports, energy-related complications and marketing claims are barriers surgeons weigh when adopting such technologies.[17]

Energy-based devices carry a risk of pigment change and scarring in darker skin. A 2023 review of treatments for Fitzpatrick skin types 4 to 6 reports that RF skin tightening devices can stimulate collagen and elastin without generating excessive surface heat, which makes them suitable for darker skin tones.[18] The 2019 RF microneedling overview likewise reports that multiple studies support minimal risks, including in dark skin types.[14]

Beyond jawline and neck work, fractional RF has been examined for periorbital wrinkles in a nonrandomized clinical trial,[19] for cellulite in a case series of the Morpheus8 body applicator,[20] for neck rejuvenation alone and with platelet-rich plasma in a randomized trial using optical coherence tomography,[15] and for alopecia areata in a randomized comparison with intralesional steroids.[21] A 2025 randomized controlled trial tested topical recombinant PDGF against standard care after RF microneedling for aesthetic outcomes and patient satisfaction.[16] A 2022 randomized trial examined ultra-thin 1 mm electrode pins for wrinkles and skin texture with clinical and histologic assessment.[22] Registered trials have also looked at RF microneedling for acne, underarm hyperhidrosis, lower eyelid edema and cellulite.[25][26][27][28]

Human evidence consists mainly of retrospective reviews, case series, small nonrandomized studies and a handful of randomized trials, many testing RF microneedling together with an adjunct. Examples include a 2020 retrospective review of combined RF treatment for lower face and neck laxity,[3] the 2019 combination series,[7] a 2021 report on jowl and neck laxity after facelift,[5] and a 2025 paper combining low-energy Morpheus8 with nanofat grafting.[8]

Randomized work includes the neck rejuvenation trial comparing RF microneedling with and without platelet-rich plasma,[15] the 2025 PDGF trial,[16] the 1 mm electrode pin trial,[22] and the alopecia areata comparison.[21] Small registered studies are listed on ClinicalTrials.gov, such as a 2019 trial in 11 patients with premature jowl and neck laxity after facelift and a 2022 study of dermal lines in 13 participants.[23][24] No randomized trial comparing Morpheus8 with surgical lifting for jawline contour has been published.
Review authors generally describe the technology as safe and effective across skin types, while the underlying studies are largely small.[4][14]
The procedure is categorized under hardmaxxing as a way to tighten and remodel tissue along the jawline and neck.

timeline.event: US FDA clearance for electrocoagulation and hemostasis; US patent for the fractional RF technology (per Grokipedia).[1]
Further FDA clearance for soft tissue contraction (per Grokipedia).[1]
